rules.fallback_text: The Argentine Constitution establishes a federal governmental structure where the provinces reserve all the powers which have not been delegated to the federal government.
Argentine private law is mainly codified in the Argentine Civil and Commercial Code, whose latest amendment entered into force on August 1st, 2015 ("CCCN").
The Argentine judicial system is divided into federal and provincial courts. The supreme judicial power is vested in the Argentine Supreme Court of Justice.
In this sense, although lower courts tend to follow decisions handed down by the higher courts (especially from the Supreme Court), their rulings are not binding.
Besides, the national legislative branch has enacted several legal statutes regarding specific fields of law (for example: Consumer Law, Employment Law, Personal Data Protection Law, Bankruptcy Law).
The criminal definitions in the ACC are not exhaustive, as several substantive laws introduced criminal offences.

The Argentine Constitution also provides for a tripartite system of government consisting of an executive branch, headed by the President, the legislative branch in the form of a Congress divided into two chambers – the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies–, and the judicial branch.

The application and effect of any law or regulation upon a particular situation can vary depending upon the specific facts and circumstances, and so you should consult with a lawyer regarding the impact of any of these regimes in any particular instance.
